The Fastrac turbine is designed to produce 895 kW of power at 20,000 RPM.
The turbine has 24 converging-diverging nozzles, 147 impulse-type shrouded blades, and 67 exit guide vanes (EGVs).
The nozzle exit Mach number is predicted to be 2.11, with a total-to-static pressure ratio of 11.2.
For the small gap case (0.102 cm), the turbine produced 890 kW of power with a work per pound of 276.3 kJ/kg.
For the large gap case (0.838 cm), the turbine produced 867 kW of power with a work per pound of 269.1 kJ/kg.
The modal analysis indicated possible resonance near the nominal design speed due to excitations from the nozzle count and EGVs.
Implementing MPI software enabled the CFD simulations to be run at the required speed.
The uncoupled nozzle and blade/EGV simulation under-predicted the losses and did not adequately capture the mixing in the axial gap region.
Highly unsteady pressures were predicted at the blade leading edge, particularly at the nozzle passing frequency and its second harmonic.
Boundary layer separation on the blade suction surface and the EGV pressure surface was observed, triggered by the wakes from the nozzle lip regions.
The small gap case showed higher unsteadiness but better aerodynamic performance compared to the large gap case.
Thick boundary layers were observed at the blade inlet for the small gap case due to the nozzle jet not fully expanding.
The large gap case had higher losses in the region between the nozzle and blade due to jet interaction.
The uncoupled simulation over-specified the inlet conditions and under-predicted the losses.
More detailed simulations of different axial spacings are planned to further understand the flow physics in this region.
